question: On initial examination of a patient with a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), the ophthalmologist identiﬁes pigment in the anterior vitreous. What additional ﬁnding during this examination increases the likelihood of discovering a retinal break?
explanation: About 7%-18% of all patients with acute symptomatic PVD have a retinal tear, and 50%-70% of PVD patients who have associated vitreous hemorrhage have retinal tears. The presence of pigment granules in the anterior vitreous ("tobacco dust") is associated with a 7-fold increase in the likelihood of ﬁnding a retinal tear. PVD usually starts a perifoveal detachment and then spreads circumferentially. A prominent Weiss ring has no bearing on the likelihood of a retinal break, nor does the presence of vitreous syneresis (which precedes PVD), or asteroid hyalosis.

question: A patient with dry age-related macular degeneration presents with new-onset decreased vision. The ophthalmologist orders ﬂuorescein angiography. A few minutes later, the patient reports that he feels short of breath and starts wheezing. This is an example of what type of hypersensitivity?
explanation: Type I hypersensitivity is triggered by the activation of IgE. Presumably, the IgE producing B lymphocytes were "primed" by prior exposure to the antigen (in this case, ﬂuorescein). The Fc portion of the IgE antibody binds to mast cells, causing them to degranulate and release interleukins and cytokines. This happens within several minutes of re- exposure. These inﬂammatory mediators can cause blood vessel dilation and massive edema, leading to reactions ranging from hives, urticarial, laryngeal edema, to ultimately, anaphylaxis. Type II hypersensitivity is deﬁned as a hypersensitivity reaction secondary to antibodies that are directly cytotoxic against human tissues. Examples of type II hypersensitivity include Goodpasture syndrome and cicatricial pemphigoid.

question: What is the typical appearance of adult-onset foveomacular dystrophy?

options.A: bilateral, coarse pigment mottling in central macula
options.C: bilateral, round or oval, yellow subfoveal lesions
options.D: bilateral ﬁshnet pattern of yellow- orange or brown pigment

explanation: Adult-onset foveomacular dystrophy presents as bilateral, round or oval, yellow subfoveal lesions. Bilateral, butterﬂy-shaped, yellow macular pigment is seen in butterﬂy- type pattern dystrophy. Fishnet pattern of yellow-orange or brown pigment is seen in reticular dystrophy. Coarse pigment mottling in central macula is seen in fundus pulverulentus.

question: What is the preferred treatment for the acute phase of serpiginous choroiditis?

options.C: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy

explanation: Serpiginous choroiditis (also termed geographic choroiditis or helicoid peripapillary choroidopathy) is a typically bilateral, chronic, progressive, recurrent inﬂammatory disease of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), choriocapillaris, and choroid; the etiology of the condition is undetermined. Local and systemic corticosteroids are the preferred therapies for the acute phase of the disorder. Demonstrating a high rate of recurrence, serpiginous choroiditis usually requires long- term anti-inﬂammatory treatment with steroid-sparing agents, such as cyclosporine A and/or azathioprine. As a deﬁnite viral etiology of serpiginous choroiditis has not been proven, antiviral therapy is not indicated. Although intravitreal anti- VEGF therapy may be beneﬁcial when serpiginous choroiditis is complicated by choroidal neovascularization (CNV), it has not been shown to be an eﬀective therapy for serpiginous choroiditis itself.

question: What feature of the choroid mitigates the potential thermal damage associated with light absorption?
explanation: The high speed of blood ﬂow through the choroid helps to dissipate thermal energy from light absorption in addition to maintaining the oxygen needs of the photoreceptors (and resulting in high oxygen tension in venous blood). The multilayer arterial structure of the choroid, which is thicker centrally than peripherally, allows blood to be delivered across the extent of the retina, with an accompanying decrease in pressure before reaching the choriocapillaris.

question: A 21-year-old man reports 4 years of trouble driving at night. He has hearing aids and an unsteady gait. The peripheral fundus of the right eye is shown in the ﬁgure. What is the ﬁnding of his serum test?
explanation: The patient has Refsum disease, which is an autosomal recessive, peroxisomal disorder characterized by a pigmentary retinopathy (seen in the ﬁgure), reduced electroretinography (ERG) responses, ichthyosis, hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia, anosmia, polyneuropathy, and cardiomyopathy. Nyctalopia may be an early sign of disease. Diagnosis is made by demonstrating elevated serum phytanic acid levels. Dietary restriction of phytanic acid foods may slow down retinal degeneration. A pigmentary retinopathy has a very large diﬀerential diagnosis. Family history in conjunction with other clinical ﬁndings helps narrow the diﬀerential diagnosis. Corneal verticillata is seen with Fabry disease and amiodarone. Tay-Sachs disease is caused by a deﬁciency of hexosaminidase A that results in glycolipid accumulation in the brain and retina. In addition to cognitive disability, the patient may develop a cherry-red spot from accumulation of whitish glycolipid in the perifoveal ganglion cells. Death usually occurs early in life. Alpha galactosidase-A is reduced in patients with Fabry disease, which is a lysosomal storage disorder that can result in conjunctival vascular abnormalities, corneal verticillata, and lens opacities.

question: A 75-year-old woman with nonexudative age-related macular degeneration complains of increasing diﬃculty reading the newspaper since her last visit 6 months earlier. Her visual acuity, examination, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) results are stable. What test results might provide a correlate to her symptom?
explanation: Compromised contrast sensitivity can be a major functional impediment that is disproportionate to visual acuity. Traditional newsprint is a relatively low-contrast target, particularly in comparison to the high-contrast Snellen chart. The Pelli-Robson test of contrast sensitivity might produce a score indicating abnormal contrast sensitivity in this patient. Although classically used to assess night blindness (nyctalopia), dark adaptometry can also reveal abnormalities in individuals with age- related macular degeneration. These deﬁcits, however, are less likely to be related to the patient’s current task-speciﬁc complaint. Similarly, photostress recovery time can be abnormal in patients with age-related BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is a posterior extension of the pars plana epithelium onto the retinal side of the ora serrata?
explanation: An enclosed ora bay is a posterior extension of the pars plana epithelium onto the retinal side of the ora serrata. A peripheral retinal excavation is thought to be a variant of lattice degeneration. A dentate process is an extension of retinal tissue extending anteriorly to the ora serrata. A meridional complex is a prominent thickening of retinal tissue that extends into the pars plana and is aligned with a ciliary process.

question: A 62-year-old woman presents with metamorphopsia in her right eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) shows a macular hole less than 400 microns in diameter. The visual acuity is 20/80. What management approach is most likely to result in improved visual acuity?

options.C: pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with peeling of the internal limiting membrane (ILM)

explanation: Stage 1 macular holes without epiretinal membrane spontaneously resolve in 50% of cases and thus are usually monitored. This patient has a stage 2 macular hole, which (like advanced stages of macular holes) requires surgical intervention, speciﬁcally pars plana vitrectomy with ILM peeling and gas tamponade, which has a success rate of over BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What clinical feature is most suggestive of Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis?

options.A: white plaque within the lens capsule
options.B: inﬂammatory cellular aggregates in the vitreous ("ﬂuﬀ balls")

explanation: A white plaque within the lens capsule following cataract surgery is associated with Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis. P acnes endophthalmitis is typically characterized by chronic, indolent, granulomatous inﬂammation. This infection is rarely eradicated with an intracapsular antibiotic injection or intravitreal antibiotic injection alone and typically requires pars plana vitrectomy with partial capsulectomy in addition to intracapsular antibiotic deposition. Diﬀuse stellate keratic BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What management is recommended for this peripheral retinal lesion for a patient with asymptomatic high myopia?
explanation: Vitreoretinal tufts without an associated retinal break can be safely observed in an asymptomatic patient. Laser retinopexy or cryopexy may be indicated in patients with retinal break associated with vitreoretinal tuft. Scleral buckle surgery may be indicated if a retinal break leads to a retinal detachment.

question: What clinical ﬁnding best characterizes Coats disease?
explanation: Coats disease is characterized by the presence of vascular dilatations (retinal telangiectasia), including ectatic arterioles, microaneurysms, venous dilations (phlebectasias), and fusiform capillary dilatations, which are frequently associated with exudative retinal detachment. Usually only 1 eye is involved, and there is a marked male predominance (85%). To date, researchers have not identiﬁed an BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test in the management of this patient?

options.B: computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography (CTA) of the brain
options.D: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and MRA of the brain

explanation: The presentation of acute-onset headache, altered mental status, third cranial nerve palsy and a vitreous hemorrhage is strongly suggestive of a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm with Terson syndrome. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) accounts for nearly 50% of cases with intracranial hemorrhage. Its incidence increases with age, and it is more common in women. African American and Hispanic individuals have a higher incidence of SAH when compared with white individuals. Most SAHs result from saccular, or "berry," aneurysms. Only a minority of cases of SAH are nonaneurysmal in etiology. Approximately 85% of congenital saccular, or "berry," aneurysms develop in the anterior part of the circle of Willis. The origin of the posterior communicating artery from the internal carotid artery is the most common site. Such an aneurysm typically presents with headache and third cranial nerve palsy involving the pupil. Vascular malformations within and on the surface of the brain parenchyma constitute approximately 7% of cases of subarachnoid hemorrhage and arise from capillary telangiectasias, cavernous hemangiomas, venous angiomas, or AVMs. SAH usually presents with abrupt onset severe headache that is typically described by patients as the "worst headache of my life." The headache occurs in 97% of cases; 30% have symptoms lateralized to the side of the hemorrhage. The combination of vitreous hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage (Terson syndrome) portends a worse prognosis. Maintaining a high index of suspicion and evaluating the patient with noncontrast CT, followed by mandatory lumbar puncture if CT results are negative, are essential in making the diagnosis. Digital subtraction angiography is superior to CT or MRA for the detection of SAH due to aneurysm. Terson syndrome is a vitreous and sub-ILM or subhyaloid hemorrhage caused by an abrupt intracranial hemorrhage. Although the exact mechanism is not known, it is suspected that the acute intracranial hemorrhage causes an acute rise in the intraocular venous pressure, resulting in a rupture of peripapillary and retinal vessels. Approximately BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: An infant is noted to have leukocoria, microphthalmos, and elongated ciliary processes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: All of the listed conditions (ROP, Coats disease, retinoblastoma) can present with leukocoria, but only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmia. PFV results from failed regression of the fetal hyaloid vasculature. Findings can vary from a retrolental membrane to a stalk connecting the lens and optic nerve. It is also associated with elongated ciliary processes, cataract and retinal detachment, and angle closure glaucoma.

question: When administered as an intravitreal injection for retinal vascular disease, what drug is most likely to cause prolonged ocular hypertension or glaucoma?
explanation: Triamcinolone acetonide, a corticosteroid, is the most likely medication of those listed to cause a prolonged increase in intraocular pressure when administered intravitreally. The other 3 medications listed (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aﬂibercept) are anti-vascular endothelial growth (anti-VEGF) agents, which, as a class, are much less likely to demonstrate this eﬀect.

question: What laboratory test should be performed in all black patients presenting with a traumatic hyphema?
explanation: Sickle cell disease is an important risk factor for hyphema among persons of African descent. In the setting of high intraocular pressure (IOP) from hyphema and sickle cell disease, IOP-lowering medications, such as acetazolamide, would be relatively contraindicated, as they may precipitate a sickle cell crisis. A hypercoagulable state may lead to bleeding in the retina due to vascular occlusion, but it is not associated with hyphema.

question: What feature characterizes West Nile virus retinopathy?

options.C: The virus can be transmitted to humans by mosquitoes.
options.D: The virus is a double-stranded DNA ﬂavivirus.

explanation: West Nile virus is typically transmitted to humans by mosquitoes. Retinopathy is an uncommon manifestation of the disease, which is caused by a single-stranded RNA ﬂavivirus. The bird serves as the primary host. The retinitis is typically bilateral. Although there is no proven treatment, the disease is usually self-limited. The visual prognosis is favorable.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and tractional retinal detachment (TRD) involving the central macula. What is the appropriate management?

options.D: pars plana vitrectomy, retinal membrane removal

explanation: The appropriate management of diabetic TRD involving or threatening the macula is pars plana vitrectomy, to eliminate vitreoretinal adhesion and subsequent traction in order to reattach the retina. Panretinal photocoagulation should precede vitrectomy if possible, but panretinal photocoagulation alone is not the appropriate treatment. Pneumatic retinopexy is used to manage rhegmatogenous retinal detachments associated with breaks in the superior 8 clock-hours, and while diabetic tractional detachments can sometimes present with combined tractional/rhegmatogenous detachments (breaks in atrophic areas), pneumatic retinopexy would be inappropriate in this scenario.

question: What useful clinical feature suggests Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome?
explanation: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is associated with alopecia, vitiligo, and poliosis in about 30% of aﬀected patients. It is more common in darkly pigmented ethnic groups and typically aﬀects patients 30 to 50 years of age. It is not associated with skin hyperpigmentation. Additional occasionally useful features are headache, stiﬀ neck, and meningismus.

question: What is a risk factor for idiopathic central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC)? &
explanation: Exogenous intake of corticosteroids, such as oral prednisone, is a risk factor for CSC. There is no known association between CSC and obesity or hydroxychloroquine use. CSC is more common in males, although there is an association between CSC and pregnancy. 8540- 492d- a62c- e460351301e5)  toxoplasmosis.

question: A 55-year-old healthy woman reports that 10 days ago, the vision in her left eye became very hazy. Then, 2 days ago, the vision in her right eye worsened as well. She also reports that her eyes have been red and painful. A fundus photo is provided. Similar lesions are noted in the peripheral retina in both eyes. What is the most likely causative agent? &
explanation: This patient has bilateral acute retinal necrosis (ARN). ARN is a necrotizing retinitis that typically presents in a healthy, immunocompetent patient with symptoms such as pain and decreased vision. ARN is bilateral in 20%-33% of patients and causative viruses include HSV, VZV, and rarely cytomegalovirus (CMV). The disease presents with a triad of severe vitritis, vasculitis, and peripheral retinitis. A peripheral, whitish, necrotizing lesion can be seen; it often spreads in a centripetal fashion peripherally, then progresses to involve the posterior pole. The risk of retinal detachment is very high. These patients have a guarded visual prognosis. Progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) is a necrotizing herpetic retinitis caused by either herpes simplex virus (HSV) or VZV. This disease, which aﬀects the outer retinal layers, is notable for a rapid progression, lack of vitritis, and sparing of retinal vessels. PORN is more frequently found in immunocompromised patients. There is a high risk of retinal detachment, frequently seen 2 - 3 months after onset.

question: What is the most likely etiology of the macular disease illustrated in the ﬁgure?
explanation: This etiology for most full-thickness macular holes is not well understood; therefore, most are classiﬁed as having an idiopathic cause. When associated with functional visual impairment, pars plana vitrectomy surgery with posterior hyaloid dissection, with or without internal limiting membrane removal, and with postoperative gas tamponade, would be preferred in most situations. Less commonly, macular holes may occur following blunt trauma. Macular holes are not directly associated with diabetes mellitus or sun gazing. 6795- de83ad7c97b6)  nuclear sclerosis.

question: After 15 years of diabetes mellitus and hypertension, a 62-year-old phakic man complains of 6 months of blurred vision in his right eye. Abnormalities are noted on his fundus and ﬂuorescein angiographic evaluations as shown. What is his most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The fundus has hard exudates in the macula of the right eye. The early ﬂuorescein angiography (FA) images conﬁrm the presence of vascular leakage and areas of capillary nonperfusion in the macula. Later images show a cystoid pattern of leakage. These ﬁndings are most consistent with diabetic macular edema. Hypertension-related retinal lesions include cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs), blot hemorrhages, lipid exudates (sometimes referred to as hard exudates), venous beading, and new retinal vessels. FA patterns of choroidal neovascularization may include classic or occult CNV or combinations of both. Classic CNV is an area of bright, lacy, and well-deﬁned hyperﬂuorescence that is identiﬁed in the early phase and progressively leaks by the late phases. Occult CNV can present as late leakage from an unidentiﬁable source. Fluorescein angiography is relatively resistant to the optical eﬀects of a cataract. Advanced cataract would decrease overall image quality. It is important for a cataract surgeon evaluating a diabetic patient with cataract to carefully consider diabetic retinopathy as an alternative cause of decreased vision.

question: What electrophysiologic diagnostic study serves as a direct measure of central retinal ganglion cell function?
explanation: The pattern electroretinogram (PERG) is the retinal response to an isoluminant alternating checkerboard stimulus presented to the macula. The stimulus is primarily alternating contrast stimulus. The responses are small, and signal averaging is needed. There are 2 main components, P50 and N95, with most subjects showing an earlier negative component, N35. N95 arises in the retinal ganglion cells N95 arises in the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and thus acts as a direct measure of central RGC (RGCs) and thus acts as a direct measure of central RGC function function. The electro-oculogram (EOG) assesses the health of the RPE by measuring the changes in the corneo-retinal standing potential during light adaptation. The multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) can be of use in the diagnosis of macular dysfunction and in assessing the extent of central retinal involvement in generalized retinal disease by producing a topographic electroretinogram (ERG) map of central retinal cone- system function. The visual evoked potential (VEP), or visual evoked response (VER), is BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What drug is most likely to cause bilateral suprachoroidal eﬀusions?
explanation: The drug topiramate is associated with suprachoroidal eﬀusions, anterior segment shallowing, and secondary angle-closure glaucoma. Sildenaﬁl has been noted to block photoreceptor signals, causing electroretinographic changes, visual disturbances (including changes in color perception), and increased light sensitivity. Doxycycline is associated with papilledema secondary to increased intracranial hypertension, or hyperpigmentation of the sclera and eyelids. Hydroxychloroquine is associated with bull's-eye maculopathy and decreased vision.

question: For a patient with age-related macular degeneration and initial, new-onset metamorphopsia, what is the most reasonable sequence of ancillary testing?

options.A: ﬂuorescein angiography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, spectral domain optical coherence tomography
options.B: fundus photography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, fundus autoﬂuorescence
options.C: spectral domain optical coherence tomography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, indocyanine green (ICG) angiography
options.D: spectral domain optical coherence tomography, then if needed for diagnostic clarity, ﬂuorescein angiography

explanation: Although controversy exists as to whether intravenous fundus ﬂuorescein angiography (FA) or optical coherence tomography (OCT) is more sensitive in detecting exudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD), FA may be necessary in this setting, as it may diagnose the retinal macroaneurysm, pseudophakic macular edema, branch retinal vein occlusion, and other confounders. However, there is no controversy about our goal to initially use the safest and least invasive diagnostic modality. Thus, the most reasonable sequence would be to do OCT before angiography in this setting. In straightforward cases, spectral domain OCT may be the only ancillary testing needed to initially diagnose a new case of exudative AMD. Once neovascularization is conﬁrmed and/or other confounders excluded, OCT is very useful to noninvasively monitor response to therapy. Fundus photography is excellent at documenting the macula examination on a particular day, but it does not provide additional diagnostic information like the other modalities listed. Autoﬂuorescence is very useful in assessing the health of the RPE and the accumulation of lipofuscin, but it is not helpful in assessing initial metamorphopsia as OCT or even FA.

question: A one-year-old boy presents with peripheral traction retinal detachment with temporal displacement of the maculae bilaterally. The child's father is similarly aﬀected. There is no history of premature birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) occurs in full-term infants and is characterized by exudative leakage and hemorrhage of the blood vessels of the temporal peripheral retina, along with incomplete vascularization of the peripheral retina. This may result in contraction of ﬁbrovascular tissue with the development of a traction retinal detachment (TRD). The condition may be inherited in an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or x-linked pattern. Congenital retinal telangiectasia and juvenile retinoschisis are not typically associated with a TRD. Incontinentia pigmenti is typically lethal in male infants.

question: What is the zoonotic vector of West Nile Virus?
explanation: West Nile viral retinopathy is caused by a single-stranded ﬂavivirus that is transmitted to humans by mosquitoes of the genus Culex. Ocular manifestations typically occur in very ill diabetic patients with encephalitis. The characteristic lesions are bilateral multifocal chorioretinitis that includes distinctive curvilinear clusters that often run parallel to the direction of the nerve ﬁber layer.

question: What ophthalmoscopic retinal ﬁnding is most characteristic of an exudative retinal detachment?

options.A: retinal detachment with a taut concave surface
options.C: subretinal ﬂuid that shifts with a change in patient position

explanation: Subretinal ﬂuid that shifts with a change in patient position is typical of an exudative retinal detachment. Retinal detachment with a taut concave surface is characteristic of a tractional retinal detachment, not an exudative retinal detachment. A corrugated appearance to the retina is most common with rhegmatogenous retinal detachments, while exudative retinal detachments usually have a smooth appearance. Fixed retinal folds typically indicate proliferative vitreoretinopathy, which is almost always secondary to a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Order a urine culture and sensitivity testing for urine color change.

question: Following ﬂuorescein angiography, what additional care is appropriate?

options.A: Order a urine culture and sensitivity testing for urine color change.
options.C: Advise the patient to avoid sunlight for 5 days after the procedure.
options.D: Observe the patient for signs of delayed adverse reactions.

explanation: Most patients tolerate ﬂuorescein angiography well without adverse eﬀects or sequelae. Simple observation of the patient for several minutes after completion of the test is suﬃcient to detect an allergic reaction. Diphenhydramine, not aspirin, is most commonly used if mild signs of allergy appear. Avoidance of sunlight is not necessary because, unlike for verteporﬁn, no increased sun sensitivity results from ﬂuorescein administration. A color change in the urine is expected as the dye exits the body and does not suggest an infection.

question: A 75-year-old man reports that the vision in his right eye dims out whenever he goes outside into bright light and that his vision slowly improves once he goes back indoors. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices that the central retinal artery ﬂashes when gentle pressure is applied to the globe. What diagnostic test should be ordered?

options.A: carotid angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) to look for carotid occlusion on the right
options.B: automated perimetry and diurnal intraocular pressure measurements
options.C: computed tomography (CT) scan looking for a compressive lesion on the right optic nerve
options.D: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan looking for enlarged extraocular muscles on the right side

explanation: Ocular ischemic syndrome is characterized by a hypotensive, ischemic retinopathy with low retinal artery pressure, poor perfusion, and midperipheral retinopathy. Ocular ischemic syndrome can cause transient or persistent blurred vision or transient visual loss upon exposure to bright light. question: A mutation of what gene in what cell type results in nonprogressive dysfunction in patients with nyctalopia and white dots?

options.A: RLBP1 gene mutation in retinal photoreceptors
options.B: ABCA4 gene mutation in retinal pigment epithelium
options.C: RDH5 gene mutation in retinal photoreceptors
options.D: RDH5 gene mutation in retinal pigment epithelium

explanation: Fundus albipunctatus is caused by a mutation in the gene RDH5. RDH5 encodes 11-cis-retinol dehydrogenase, a microsomal enzyme in the RPE that converts 11-cis-retinol into 11-cis-retinal and is therefore involved in the regeneration of rhodopsin. Patients with mutations in this gene have very delayed rhodopsin regeneration, and although levels eventually normalize, the process can take many hours in the dark. Mutations in the gene RLBP1 result in retinitis punctata albescens. ABCA4 is a gene that, depending on the exact mutation, can cause Stargardt disease, fundus ﬂavimaculatus, cone-rod dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), among others.

question: What is the most likely causative organism of endogenous endophthalmitis associated with diabetic liver abscess?
explanation: Klebsiella species is the most common cause of endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with liver abscesses. Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species are the most common causes of endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with endocarditis. Escherichia coli is a common cause of endogenous endophthalmitis in patients with urinary tract infections.

question: A patient presents with an elevated lesion on dilated fundus examination. The B-scan is shown in Figure 1 and the A-scan is shown in Figure 2. What is the most likely lesion?
explanation: This imaging is most consistent with a circumscribed choroidal hemangioma. These hemangiomas are usually orange, dome-shaped lesions that can be associated with exudative retinal detachments, which can aﬀect vision if the fovea is involved. A-scan ultrasonography demonstrated high internal reﬂectivity, as illustrated in the photo. A choroidal detachment can sometimes be dome shaped but usually has low internal reﬂectivity. Choroidal melanoma demonstrates low internal reﬂectivity and can also demonstrate choroidal excavation. Choroidal osteomas often cause acoustic shadowing secondary to calcium.

question: A 67-year-old patient undergoes uneventful cataract surgery in the right eye. Five (5) days after surgery, the patient experiences an abrupt onset of painless and profound vision loss in the operated eye and has the fundus appearance shown. What intracameral antibiotic is implicated in this condition?
explanation: Hemorrhagic occlusive retinal vasculitis (HORV) is a rare but potentially visually devastating condition that can occur after the intraocular injection of vancomycin. A similar complication has not been observed with other antibiotics administered intracamerally. Any antibiotic solutions prepared for intracameral use should be preservative-free, as toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS) has been reported after intracameral injection of antibiotics containing preservatives. posterior embryotoxon.

question: What other ocular ﬁnding is most likely to be observed in the eye shown in the ﬁgure?
explanation: The ﬁgure shows a ﬁbrovascular stalk arising from the optic nerve and coursing through the vitreous towards the lens. This is an example of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), which results from failure of regression of the primary vitreous and hyaloid artery. This condition is typically sporadic and unilateral. Its presentation varies from Bergmeister papillae or Mittendorf dot in the milder cases to a microphthalmic eye with retrolental plaque in more severe cases. Often elongated ciliary processes may be observed. The ﬁbrovascular stalk can exert traction onto the retina and lead to retinal detachment. Cataract may also form and may require early cataract extraction with membrane excision. c84e- 4ece- 8d30- ef838e230eb5)  aortic dissection.

question: What systemic disease causes the fundus appearance shown in the image? 62fd- 4c54- b6da- d2dfee7b9673&t=636716580789730000)  megalocornea B.
explanation: Systemic hypertension may cause retinopathy, choroidopathy, and optic neuropathy. The most severe manifestation is optic neuropathy, which presents as optic disc edema, hemorrhages, and ischemia. Optic disc manifestations suggest a sustained and highly elevated systolic blood pressure, often above 200 mm Hg. Ocular ischemic syndrome comprises the ocular symptoms and signs attributable to chronic severe ocular hypoperfusion caused by ipsilateral carotid obstruction or ophthalmic artery obstruction. Typical ﬁndings include narrowed arteries, dilated by not very tortuous veins, hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and neovascularization of the optic nerve head, retina, or both. Diabetic retinopathy is characterized by intraretinal hemorrhages, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, and dilation and beading of retinal veins. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is deﬁned by extraretinal ﬁbrovascular proliferation. Aortic dissection is associated with Marfan syndrome and does not have a characteristic fundus appearance.

question: For this asymptomatic, 35-year-old man with a corrected visual acuity of 20/20 OU and the fundus shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The image demonstrates macular drusen. In an asymptomatic 35-year- old patient, the most likely diagnosis is familial dominant drusen, which could be conﬁrmed by examination of ﬁrst-degree relatives. Other less likely diagnoses would include cuticular drusen (basal laminar drusen), Sorsby macular dystrophy, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient presents with a suspected open-globe injury from a construction accident. The patient is unsure what hit his eye. Vision from the eye is light perception only. External examination reveals a total hyphema and 360 degrees of subconjunctival hemorrhage. The patient has not had anything to eat or drink in at least 8 hours. What is the best next step in management?

options.A: immediate globe exploration in the operating room
options.B: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits
options.C: placement of a fox shield on the eye and a plan for immediate globe exploration and possible repair of open globe
options.D: computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain and orbits

explanation: The ﬁrst step in a suspected open-globe injury should be a CT scan of the brain and orbits. A CT scan will evaluate the shape of the globe and help identify an intraocular foreign body (IOFB). Additionally, it can identify other head and facial trauma. MRI is helpful for identifying wood or glass foreign bodies that may be diﬃcult to detect on CT. However, if a metallic foreign body is suspected, as in this case in a construction accident, MRI should be avoided, because movement of a metallic IOFB could cause additional damage. Although immediate globe exploration in the operating room can be performed, it is inferior to CT scan and risks causing extrusion of ocular contents. question: In the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS), what therapy was demonstrated to be safe and eﬀective for the treatment of the condition illustrated? placement of a fox shield on the eye and a plan for immediate globe exploration and possible repair of open globe C.

options.C: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy

explanation: The ETDRS demonstrated the eﬃcacy of focal laser photocoagulation for diabetic macular edema (DME). Although intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor therapy, intravitreal corticosteroid therapy, and vitrectomy surgery might demonstrate eﬃcacy in the management of DME, the ETDRS preceded these therapies, and they were not evaluated in the study.

question: In an eye with retinoschisis, what examination ﬁndings are associated with an increased risk of progression to retinal detachment?
explanation: The presence of inner and outer layer breaks in retinoschisis is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment. However, the presence of outer layer breaks (but not inner breaks) can lead to a localized retinal detachment that usually does not progress and seldom requires treatment. The presence of a bullous inner layer does not predispose to retinal detachment. Finally, the presence of a demarcation line in an eye with retinoschisis indicates that a chronic localized retinal detachment is present or has spontaneously regressed; this is not likely to lead to a progressive retinal detachment.

question: A 2-week-old infant with leukocoria is suspected of having persistent fetal vasculature (PFV). Anatomically, what globe size strongly supports a diagnosis of PFV over retinoblastoma?
explanation: Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) results from the failure of the fetal hyaloid vascular complex to regress and is almost always unilateral. Clinically, a retrolental membrane of varying size and density is attached to the posterior lens surface. In contrast to retinoblastoma, which typically occurs in normal-sized eyes, these eyes are nearly always microphthalmic (small and disorganized globe) to some degree. Nanophthalmos refers to small eyes (axial length < 18 mm ) that have a high lens-to-anterior segment ratio but otherwise lack disorganization. Buphthalmos ("ox eye") refers to diﬀuse globe enlargement, usually in the setting of congenital glaucoma.

question: What electrophysiologic test best evaluates the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?
explanation: The electro-oculogram (EOG), an electrophysiologic test for evaluating the RPE, measures the trans-RPE potential. The electroretinogram (ERG) measures electrical changes in the retina in response to a light stimulus (Figure). The a-waves and b-waves, 2 of the major components of the ERG waveform, correspond to the electrical response in the outer retina (photoreceptors) and inner retina (bipolar and Müller cells), respectively. The c-wave of the ERG can be used to study the RPE but is not typically employed clinically. Oscillatory potentials, seen on the ERG, are responses from the inner retina that are used in the evaluation of retinal vascular disease. Multifocal ERG is used to evaluate individual areas of the macula, and the pattern ERG focuses on retinal ganglion cell function. Visual evoked potential (VEP) measures the changes that occur at the occipital cortex following light stimulation and assesses the aﬀerent visual system. c327- 486d-.

question: What ciliopathy is associated with pigmentary retinopathy and hearing loss?
explanation: Ciliopathies are diseases or syndromes in which a mutation in a gene needed for ciliary function aﬀects multiple organ systems. Usher syndrome is a ciliopathy deﬁned by the association of retinitis pigmentosa with congenital sensorineural hearing loss. Bardet-Biedl syndrome is a ciliopathy with ﬁndings that include pigmentary retinopathy and bull’s-eye maculopathy, obesity, polydactyly, hypogonadism, renal disease, and cognitive disability. Joubert syndrome is a ciliopathy characterized by cerebellar malformation BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What term best describes the vision loss in cone dystrophy?
explanation: Patients with cone dystrophy present with progressive loss of visual acuity and color discrimination, often accompanied by hemeralopia (day blindness) and photophobia (discomfort and/or pain in the presence of normal levels of light). Onset of symptoms typically occurs in the teenage years or later adulthood. Ophthalmoscopy may be normal early in the course of the disease. Because of this, patients with cone dystrophies may be suspected of malingering. In other patients, ophthalmoscopy may reveal the typical symmetric bull’s-eye pattern of BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What bilateral white dot syndrome is characterized by profound vision loss typically followed by full or near-full vision recovery?

options.D: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

explanation: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) is an uncommon, usually bilateral inﬂammatory disorder characterized by acute onset visual loss, usually followed weeks to months later by substantial or near-complete improvement. On FA, APMPPE (also known as AMPPE or AMPPPE) in the acute phase demonstrates a characteristic fundus pattern of early lesion blockage, followed by lesion staining in the middle and late phases. No treatment has been demonstrated to aﬀect the time or ﬁnal outcome of recovery. Birdshot uveitis is characterized by insidious onset and chronic progression. Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a unilateral syndrome with decreased vision, scotomas, and sometimes photopsias, with improvement over 2-6 weeks without treatment. Serpiginous chorioretinopathy is typically relentlessly progressive, and destroys the RPE on photoreceptors. Thus, recovery of vision, even following immunosuppression, is atypical.

question: A 29-year-old man presents for routine ophthalmic examination. He notes poor vision in his left eye for as long as he can remember, but he has never had an eye examination in the past. Visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/100 in the left eye. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye is unremarkable. Fundus examination of the left eye is depicted in the ﬁgure. What would a ﬂuorescein angiogram, if performed, be most likely to demonstrate?

options.A: hyperﬂuorescence secondary to diﬀuse leakage throughout the lesion
options.C: no leakage, as well as a gravitational plasma-erythrocyte separation

explanation: The ﬁgure depicts a retinal cavernous hemangioma, which is a benign hamartoma. Most cases are sporadic, although a familial, autosomal dominant pattern has been seen in conjunction with skin and intracranial hemangiomas. Clinically, a retinal cavernous hemangioma appears as a grape-like cluster of thin-walled saccular angiomatous lesions in the inner retina or optic nerve. They are typically located peripherally and are asymptomatic (this patient has a severe case involving the central vision that is less common). Rarely, the hemangiomas may bleed into the vitreous. This lesion should be on the diﬀerential diagnosis of any patient with a vitreous hemorrhage of unknown etiology. In addition, cavernous hemangiomas are one of the conditions that can cause subretinal, intraretinal, and preretinal hemorrhage. Blood ﬂow through the lesions is slow. Fluorescein angiography typically shows no leakage and may show gravitational plasma-erythrocyte separation. Subretinal edema and exudate is uncommon. Most lesions are observed unless they cause vision loss, in which case cryotherapy or photocoagulation may be considered. If severe vitreous hemorrhage occurs, pars plana vitrectomy is an option.

question: Peripheral retinal excavations are a risk factor for what disorder?
explanation: Tears may occur at the site of peripheral retinal excavations, which in turn may lead to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Peripheral retinal excavations may represent a mild form of lattice degeneration, with associated ﬁrm vitreoretinal adhesions. They are often aligned with meridional folds. These lesions have no known association with retinoschisis, peripheral cystic degeneration, or cobblestone degeneration.

question: A patient with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes presents with vision loss (20/200) in 1 eye. Clinical examination shows mild inferior vitreous hemorrhage, minimal macular edema outside of the central macula, and a well- perfused optic nerve. Fluorescein angiography demonstrates an area of neovascularization elsewhere and a foveal avascular zone (FAZ) of 1500 microns. What is the most likely cause of poor vision?
explanation: Vision loss in patients with diabetic retinopathy can be associated with the abnormalities that include capillary leakage, ischemic maculopathy (capillary occlusion), and sequelae from ischemia-induced neovascularization. Vitreous hemorrhage, macular edema, tractional detachment, and ischemic maculopathy can all cause vision loss. In the above vignette, ischemic maculopathy (FAZ ~1500 microns) is the most likely cause, since the vitreous hemorrhage is outside of the visual axis (inferior) and the macular edema is noncentral. 1 50 per pag.

question: In a patient with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), what is an indication to initiate Age-Related Eye Disease Study [AREDS] vitamin therapy?
explanation: In the original AREDS and in AREDS2, participants who beneﬁted from antioxidant vitamin and mineral supplementation were those who had either intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in 1 eye. For participants with extensive intermediate (ie, medium-sized) drusen in 1 or both eyes, 1 or more large drusen in at least 1 eye, nonsubfoveal geographic atrophy in 1 eye, or advanced AMD (ie, subfoveal geographic atrophy or choroidal neovascularization [CNV]) in 1 eye who had been assigned to the group using the combination treatment of antioxidant vitamins with zinc and copper, the rate of development of advanced AMD at 5 BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What type of hemorrhage is most characteristic of Valsalva retinopathy?
explanation: Sub-ILM hemorrhage is typical of Valsalva retinopathy. A sudden rise in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure (such as accompanies coughing, vomiting, lifting, or straining for a bowel movement) might raise intraocular venous pressure suﬃciently to rupture small superﬁcial capillaries in the macula. It is typically self-limiting, not requiring prompt surgical intervention, and has a good visual prognosis.

question: For a patient with initial onset of symptoms due to central serous choroidopathy, what is the preferred management?
explanation: Central serous chorioretinopathy typically resolves spontaneously within weeks to months of onset. Persistent, symptomatic cases may respond to thermal laser photocoagulation and/or verteporﬁn photodynamic therapy. Systemic corticosteroid therapy may exacerbate the condition, as may systemic conditions associated with elevated serum cortisol levels.

question: What systemically administered drug can result in a complication of a pigmentary retinopathy?
explanation: The taxanes (docetaxel, paclitaxel) and niacin can induce a microcystic form of macular edema that is detected on SD-OCT and does not leak on ﬂuorescein angiography. The phenothiazine thioridazine can cause a severe pigmentary retinopathy that can develop within a few weeks or months of high-dose utilization. Toxicity is rare with thioridazine doses of less than 800 mg/day.

question: What cause of leukocoria is associated with microphthalmos?
explanation: Each of the answer choices (Coats disease, retinoblastoma, persistent fetal vasculature, and Toxocara species) can cause unilateral leukocoria. However, only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmos. Additionally, it is associated with elongated ciliary processes, cataract, retinal detachment, and angle-closure glaucoma.

question: A 70-year-old man with no prior ocular history presents with 0.5+ anterior chamber cells and 2+ anterior chamber ﬂare. Intraocular pressure is 10 mm Hg. question: What surgical practice improves the prognosis for hole closure for a stage 3 full-thickness macular hole?

options.A: delaying surgery by several months after symptom onset
options.B: peeling of the inner limiting membrane

explanation: Peeling of the inner limiting membrane (ILM), particularly in surgeries for stage 3 and 4 macular holes, has been demonstrated to improve the rate of hole closure. Peeling of the cortical vitreous is a common feature of vitrectomy for multiple macular diseases. Vitrectomy is BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 23-year-old man presents with poor night vision and peripheral vision loss for several years. Fundus examination is shown in the image below. The patient's mother is unaﬀected by the disease, and he is unaware of his father's medical history because his mother remarried shortly after he was born. question: In the modiﬁed Scheie classiﬁcation of hypertensive retinopathy, what grade is deﬁned by the presence of obvious narrowing with some focal irregularities and arteriovenous crossing changes?
explanation: Multiple systems for grading hypertensive retinopathy exist, including the modiﬁed Scheie classiﬁcation, the Keith-Wagener-Barker classiﬁcation, and the Wong-Mitchell classiﬁcation. The Wong-Mitchell classiﬁcation is a simpliﬁed version of the K-W-B system that considers the implications of retinal ﬁndings for systemic risk stratiﬁcation. The modiﬁed Scheie classiﬁcation is in widespread use and is deﬁned as: Grade 0: No changes Grade 1: Barely detectable arterial narrowing Grade 2: Obvious arterial narrowing with focal irregularities Grade 3: Grade 2 plus retinal hemorrhages and/or exudates Grade 4: Grade 3 plus optic nerve head swelling % A. 94% A. 94% B. 0% B. 0% C. 2% C. 2% D. 0% D. 0% Explanation & Notes Discussion BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What condition is a contraindication to B-scan echography?
explanation: Endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, and magnetic intraocular foreign body are not contraindications for ocular ultrasonography. However, if there is any suspicion for open ocular wounds (such as a large corneoscleral laceration), gonioscopy, scleral depression, and ultrasonography should all be avoided to prevent prolapse of intraocular structures.

question: A 62-year-old man with a history of trabeculectomy in the right eye 1 year prior presents with pain and decreased vision in the right eye. On examination, he has diﬀuse conjunctival hyperemia, purulent material within the bleb, and 2+ cell in the anterior chamber and vitreous cavity. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.C: intravitreal antibiotics with or without pars plana vitrectomy

explanation: This patient has bleb-related endophthalmitis, which often occurs many years after trabeculectomy. While blebitis is characterized by mucopurulent inﬁltrate within the bleb, localized conjunctival hyperemia, and minimal to no intraocular inﬂammation, bleb-related endophthalmitis has more diﬀuse conjunctival hyperemia, purulent material within the bleb, and prominent anterior chamber inﬂammation. A hypopyon or vitritis may also be present. While blebitis may be treated with topical or subconjunctival antibiotics, bleb-related endophthalmitis is treated like other types of endophthalmitis, with intravitreal injection of antibiotics. Because organisms associated with bleb-related endophthalmitis are often more virulent, early vitrectomy may be considered. Topical steroids alone are not appropriate for treating endophthalmitis. 353c- 4ebd- 924d- 178957cfa3e3)  peripheral retinoschisis A. 2% macular hole B. 90%.

question: A 62-year-old woman presents with decreased central vision. An optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan is performed and the image is shown below. What complication is most likely to occur? topical antibiotics A.
explanation: The clinical presentation described is consistent with the vitreomacular traction syndrome (VMT), also known as vitreomacular adhesion (VMA). VMT is a disorder of the vitreoretinal interface, characterized by (a) an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), (b) an abnormally strong adherence of the posterior hyaloid face to the macula, and (c) anteroposterior traction exerted by the vitreous pulling at adherent sites on the macula, causing morphologic and possible visual symptoms. Focal attachment of the vitreous to the foveola can induce foveal cavitation and macular hole formation. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments can be caused by retinal breaks or tears that form during a posterior vitreous detachment. The scan shows VMT and an incomplete PVD, so this would be less likely. VMT is not directly related to the development of choroidal neovascularization or peripheral retinoschisis.

question: What property of indocyanine green allows for imaging of the choroidal vasculature?

options.B: It freely diﬀuses through the fenestrations of the choriocapillaris.
options.C: It ﬂuoresces in the ultraviolet range.
options.D: It is almost completely protein bound after intravenous injection.

explanation: Indocyanine green angiography is useful because it is able to delineate deeper structures in the choroid, since the tricarbocyanine dye is almost completely protein bound (98%). This is in contrast to ﬂuorescein, which freely diﬀuses. ICG is water-soluble. ICG's excitation and emissions peaks are in the near-infrared range.

question: Intravitreal bevacizumab has demonstrated eﬃcacy in the management of diabetic macular edema and what other ophthalmic disorder?
explanation: Anti–vascular epithelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) drugs, including bevacizumab, have been shown to be eﬃcacious in treatment of choroidal neovascular membrane. Bevacizumab has no role in treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal eﬀusion.

question: Histoplasma capsulatum infection most commonly occurs in what geographic area?
explanation: The highest prevalence of H capsulatum exposure is in the Mississippi and Ohio River watersheds. Although the Missouri River is a branch of the Mississippi, H capsulatum has not been found endemic to its valley. Coccidioidomycosis, which can be found in the San Joaquin Valley as well as in the soil of several southwestern states, Mexico, and Central and South America, may mimic the clinical features of presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome ("punched-out" small chorioretinal scars, peripapillary scarring). This disorder is due to the fungus Coccidioides, not H capsulatum. question: What disorder can be associated with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas?
explanation: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is characterized by retinal capillary hemangioblastomas in association with angiomatous lesions of the central nervous system and cysts and tumors in the viscera. Manifestations include cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pancreatic cysts, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma. Diﬀuse choroidal hemangioma is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalofacial hemangiomatosis), whereas circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas have no systemic disease or syndrome association. Retinal astrocytic hamartomas, or retinal astrocytomas, are benign lesions and may be associated with tuberous sclerosis or neuroﬁbromatosis type 1. On the other hand, central nervous system astrocytomas can be malignant tumors. Retinal arterial macroaneurysms are associated with idiopathic systemic hypertension and atherosclerotic disease.

question: What is the most common cause of vision loss due to ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)?
explanation: The most common cause of vision loss in OHS is CNV. If 1 eye with OHS has CNV, then the risk that the other eye will develop visual loss is 1% if there are no ﬁndings of OHS in the fellow eye; 4% if there is peripapillary atrophy in the fellow eye; and 25% if focal macular histo spots are present. The treatment of CNV in OHS includes photodynamic therapy or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti- VEGF) therapy. Inﬂammatory vitreous opacities and retinal vasculitis are absent in OHS. The classic peripheral punched-out chorioretinal scars of OHS typically do not cause vision loss.

question: One month ago, a 25-year-old woman experienced transient visual loss. Two days ago, she noted a smudge in the central vision of her right eye. Her visual acuity is 20/40 eccentrically OD and 20/20 OS. Her pupils react briskly without a relative aﬀerent pupillary defect. Her left fundus is normal. Given that her right fundus is abnormal as shown, what ﬁnding might be expected?

options.A: inferior altitudinal visual ﬁeld defect OD
options.B: scotoma on Amsler grid testing OD
options.D: choroidal hypoﬂuorescence on ﬂuorescein angiography OD

explanation: This patient has multiple retinal hemorrhages, disc edema, cotton-wool spots, and tortuous veins from a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). The absence of a relative aﬀerent pupillary defect strongly suggests that this is a nonischemic CRVO. However, the reduction in visual acuity would likely be associated with macular edema, which would result in a central scotoma on Amsler grid testing. A superior branch retinal vein occlusion would be associated with an inferior altitudinal defect, but this ﬁnding would not be likely in a nonischemic CRVO. In CRVO, color vision should be relatively intact. Intravenous ﬂuorescein angiography would show delayed venous ﬁlling, staining of the retinal veins, and hypoﬂuorescence corresponding to regions of retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots. Choroidal hypoﬂuorescence would not be associated with a CRVO.

question: A 78-year-old pseudophakic man from a nursing home presented with severe pain and visual acuity of 20/100. He was diagnosed with endophthalmitis with culture showing streptococcal species. What part of this history portends a good prognosis?

options.D: relatively good visual acuity at presentation

explanation: Severe cases of endophthalmitis are correlated with loss of red fundus reﬂex, aﬀerent pupillary defect, and poor vision at the time of initial presentation. Lens status and living condition are not signiﬁcant risk prognosticators. 90.

question: Within the retina, the density of rods is greatest at what degree of ﬁxation?
explanation: The rod photoreceptors have their greatest density (about 160,000 rods/mm ) within the retina at around 12 degrees of ﬁxation. Rod density decreases toward the peripheral retina. Cone density is greatest (around 140,000 cones/mm ) in the fovea. Within the central fovea, only cones are observed. The fovea is deﬁned as a concave central retinal depression seen on slit-lamp examination; it is approximately 1.5 mm in diameter. 2 2

question: An area of peripheral retina demonstrates pathologic changes of inner retinal atrophy, retinal vascular sclerosis, and condensation and adherence of vitreous to the margins, with an overlying pocket of liqueﬁed vitreous. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Lattice peripheral retinal degeneration histopathologically demonstrates pathologic ﬁndings of a localized area of inner retinal atrophy with loss of the internal limiting membrane, adherent vitreous to the edges of the lesion with an overlying pocket of liqueﬁed vitreous, and sclerosis of the remaining retinal vessels as shown (ﬁgures): Figure 1 Figure 1: Lattice degeneration may present as prominent sclerotic vessels (arrows) in a wicker or lattice pattern. The clinical presentation has many variations. Figure 2 Figure 2: The vitreous directly over lattice degeneration is liqueﬁed (asterisk), but formed vitreous remains adherent at the margins (arrowheads) of the degenerated area. The internal limiting membrane is discontinuous, and the inner retinal layers are atrophic. These pathologies give rise to the "lattice" of sclerotic vessels that cross the lesion. Lattice retinal degeneration is seen in approximately 10% of the population, but it rarely leads to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Lattice degeneration is, however, present in 20% to 40% of rhegmatogenous detachments. Traction from the adherent vitreous can lead to a ﬂap retinal tear with persistent vitreoretinal traction. The liqueﬁed vitreous can move to the subretinal space if a full-thickness retinal hole develops. Radial perivascular lattice degeneration is similar histopathologically; however, it is seen more posteriorly along the retinal vessels. It is more common in hereditary vitreoretinal degenerations, such as Stickler syndrome. In contrast, paving stone degeneration is due to outer retinal ischemia, presumably from occlusions of the choriocapillaris. A scalloped area of retinal atrophy (cobblestone, paving-stone) develops, with dense adhesions of the inner retina to Bruch membrane. Because of the dense adhesion, retinal detachments do not occur in these areas.
